Panel’s Decision
 
THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council as the consent authority, is satisfied that the matters required to be addressed under Clause 4.6(3) of the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014 have been demonstrated and that consent may be granted to the development application, which contravenes the Height of Buildings and Floor Space Ratio development standards under Clauses 4.3 and 4.4E  of Woollahra LEP 2014.
 
AND 
 
THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, grant development consent to Development Application No. 148/2025/1 for substantial demolition of existing dwelling and construction of a new dwelling on land at 11A Wentworth Street Point Piper.
 
Reasons for Decision
 
The Panel has undertaken a site orientation, considered submissions and reviewed the assessment report prepared by Council officers that addresses the relevant matters detailed in Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.
 
For the reasons generally in the assessment report, the Panel is satisfied that the application can be approved subject to the Conditions as set out in the Attachment including the addition of Condition F.28 requiring the provision of a canopy tree consistent with Council’s Landscape Referral Response  (Adopted Conditions of Consent)

Note:Isabelle Shapiro declared a Non-Significant, Non-Pecuniary Interest in this item as Isabelle Shapiro knows Brett Daintry, who is an objector as she worked with him when she was a  Woollahra Councillor and Mr. Daintry a Manager at Council.  Isabelle Shapiro took part  in the Site Inspection, briefing session, debated and voted on this matter.

Note:Late correspondence was tabled by Dominic Wang, Thomass Wong, Team Leader, AE Design Partnership and Brett Daintry.

Note:Zein Hassan, Objector and Lucretia Liu, Planner and Natalie Scipioni, Architect addressed the Panel.

 


Panel’s Decision

 

THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, is satisfied that the matters required to be addressed under Clause 4.6(3) of the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014 have been demonstrated and that consent may be granted to the development application, which contravenes the Height of buildings development standard under Clause 4.3 of Woollahra LEP 2014.

 

AND 

 

THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, grant development consent to Development Application No. 547/2024/1 for alterations and additions to the existing dwelling on land at 13 Belah Avenue VAUCLUSE.

 

Reasons for Decision

 

The Panel has undertaken a site orientation, considered submissions, late correspondence  and reviewed the assessment report prepared by Council officers that addresses the relevant matters detailed in Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act

1979.

 

The Panel either amended or added Conditions relating to the landscaping, fencing, cabana, roof terrace and structural adequacy.  These Conditions were imposed on the grounds of ensuring equitable view sharing (including from the public domain), and ensuring acceptable residential amenity is maintained to adjoining properties.

 

For the reasons generally in the assessment report, the Panel is satisfied that the application

can be approved subject to the Conditions as set out in the Attachment (Adopted Conditions

of Consent)

  


Note: In accordance with the Woollahra Local Planning Panel Operational Procedures the votes are recorded on this planning matter.

For the MotionAgainst the Motion

Panel’s Decision

 

THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, refuse to grant development consent to DA263/2025/1 for the demolition of an automotive service premises and the construction of a shop top housing development comprising commercial and retail premises, three residential units and basement car parking on land at 77-79 New South Head Road Vaucluse, for the reasons outlined in Attachment 2.

 

Reasons for Decision

 

The Panel has undertaken a site inspection, considered the submissions and reviewed the 

assessment report prepared by Council officers that addresses the relevant matters detailed in 

Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.  

 

The Panel is satisfied that the application be refused for the reasons set out in Attachment  (Adopted Reasons for Refusal).

 


Note: In accordance with the Woollahra Local Planning Panel Operational Procedures the votes are recorded on this planning matter.

Panel’s Decision
 
THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, is satisfied that the matters required to be addressed under Clause 4.6(3) of the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014 have been demonstrated and that consent may be granted to the development application, which contravenes the Height of Buildings and Floor Space Ratio development standards under Clauses 4.3 and 4.4E of Woollahra LEP 2014.
 
AND 
 
THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, grant development consent to DA190/2025/1 for Alterations and additions to the existing dwelling house including a new lift on land at 60 Wunulla Road POINT PIPER.
 
Reasons for Decision
 
The Panel has undertaken a site orientation and reviewed the assessment report prepared by Council officers that addresses the relevant matters detailed in Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.
 
For the reasons generally in the assessment report, the Panel is satisfied that the application can be approved subject to the Conditions as set out in the Attachment (Adopted Conditions of Consent)

Note: In accordance with the Woollahra Local Planning Panel Operational Procedures the votes are recorded on this planning matter.

Kerry Kyriacou
Isabelle Shapiro


4/0

Councillor Price:

  • Acknowledgement of OPUS and the Tourgelis Family
Councillor Price acknowledged and thanked OPUS and the Tourgelis family for their extraordinary contribution to the Paddington community.

Councillor Price advised that, after 57 years in Paddington, OPUS has sadly announced it will be closing its doors. Established in 1968, OPUS became a much-loved business for both locals and visitors alike.

The business has been proudly owned and operated by the Tourgelis family for 47 years. Current owners, Chris Tourgelis and his sister, Irene Mihailou, have continued the legacy begun by their parents, who purchased the store in 1978 when Chris was just ten years old.

OPUS began as a small shopfront in Ormond Street, later moving to Oxford Street, including a period in the shopfront outside the historic Juniper Hall. When those shopfronts were demolished in the 1980s to make way for the restoration of Juniper Hall, OPUS moved to 344 Oxford Street, before then relocating further up Oxford Street to the art deco style double storey ‘York House’ building at number 354.

More than just a gift store, OPUS was a fabulous emporium -a treasure trove of quirky greeting cards, creative homewares and unique finds, long before this kind of retail concept became common. It was, in every sense, ahead of its time.

Beyond its retail success, OPUS has always been a generous supporter of the local community - contributing to countless Paddington events and fundraisers. During my time as P&C President at Glenmore Road Public School, I experienced first-hand their generosity and willingness to help whenever asked. OPUS enthusiastically participated in the inaugural postcode celebration of 2021 and for a time, Chris was President of the Paddington Business Chamber.  

 

Chris and Irene also took OPUS into the digital age expanding to a successful online store, while maintaining the same warmth and connection that made their physical store so beloved.

On behalf of Woollahra Council and the Paddington community, I extend our deepest thanks to the Tourgelis family for their contribution to Paddington for close to five decades. 

OPUS will be dearly missed but its joyful legacy will remain part of Paddington’s story for many years to come.

The Mayor also conveyed her congratulations to OPUS and the Tourgelis family and will formally express them in a letter.

Councillor Jarvis: 

  • Bellevue Hill’s Heritage
  • Australian Industry & Defence Network

Councillor Jarvis advised that last month it was a special treat to join Nick Jordan of the Historic Houses Association of Australia (HHA) on his guided walking tour of the built and natural heritage along Ginahgulla and Trahlee Roads in Bellevue Hill. Councillor Jarvis and Councillor Woodgate were able to trace the architectural styles of Sydney starting with the 1858 Victorian Revival ‘Fairfax House’ now the Scots boarding house, a rare glimpse inside Rona another Gothic revival building, built a bit later in 1883 with it’s magnificent garden. However the gem for Councillor Jarvis was the Professor Leslie Wilkinson designed Silchester Apartments built around 1930. That has relevance to the Woollahra Council's Wilkinson Heritage study where last year we listed another 5 Wilkinson buildings as local heritage items.

Councillor Jarvis further advised that on 1 October 2025 she represented the Mayor at the Australian Industry & Defence Network Gala Dinner. Our community is closely connected to Navy training and capability with HMAS Watson located in our Council and in Vaucluse Ward. A highlight was meeting last year's winner of the Young Achievers Award, Renee Aqualina for her work leading the Digital design team at DroneShield.

Councillor Torsten:

  • Cooper Park Community Garden Christmas Party
  • German Cultural Festival

Councillor Torsten invited all Councillors to the upcoming Cooper Park Community Garden Christmas, Chanukah, Summer Solstice Party on 16 November 2025 where Councillors will be able to see the rebuilt garden which was recently completed one month ahead of schedule.

Councillor Torsten further advised that he recently attended the German Cultural Festival at the Goethe-Institut. Councillor Torsten praised the festival and recommended that it become an annual event.

The Mayor extended her congratulations to the organisers of the German Cultural Festival, in particular to Christoph Mücher and the German Consul General Felix Schwarz.

Councillor Robertson:

  • Acknowledgement of OPUS and the Tourgelis Family

Councillor Robertson added to Councillor Price’s remarks, reiterating his congratulations to OPUS and the Tourgelis family for their outstanding contribution.

Councillor Carmichael:

  • October 7 Memorial Event

Councillor Carmichael advised that he, along with the Mayor attended the second anniversary memorial event held in Rodney Reserve, Dover Heights. Councillor Carmichael noted that the event drew over 7,000 community members from across many different areas.

Councillor Carmichael stated that the gathering was less about mourning and focused more on anticipation, remembrance, unity, and growing together.

Councillor Carmichael shared that several members of the Jewish community had spoken with him during the event, expressing a sense of relief and saying they could finally “exhale” after a prolonged period of anxiety.

Councillor Carmichael extended his gratitude to Woollahra Council for hosting both this year’s and last year’s memorials, and acknowledged the appreciation shown by attendees towards Council staff for their support

The Mayor added by saying that the memorial was a very moving and important event, and shared Councillor Carmichael's sentiments.

The Mayor, Councillor Dixson:

  • Queen Street & West Woollahra Event
  • Eastern Suburbs Police Area Command Awards

The Mayor congratulated the Queen Street & West Woollahra Association on a fabulous day of fashion held on 16 October 2025. The Mayor extended her congratulations in particular to Mary Read for her organisation of the event. The Mayor expressed that the fashion show was a wonderful display of all of what Woollahra has to offer in the fashion, jewellery and accessories scene. The Mayor expressed her appreciation to the businesses that donated clothing, and extended her thanks to the two modelling agencies whose contribution of models elevated the event to a very high standard.

The Mayor added that the lunch held after the event at Bistro Moncur was excellent, informative and engaging, and very well attended. The Mayor extended her thanks to the Woollahra Hotel for their contribution to the Queen Street & West Woollahra Association event.

On 20 October 2025, the Mayor attended the Eastern Suburbs Police Area Command Awards Day and congratulated the award recipients. The Mayor acknowledged that the Awards Day is an annual event where our first line of defence are recognised, as well as community members who do some seriously extraordinary things. The Mayor stated that with each year she attends these award ceremonies, the more and more impressed she is with the stories she hears. The Mayor reflected on a number of unbelievable things that have happened in recent years, and that these award ceremonies are a great occasion to recognise what the Police do every day. The Mayor acknowledged that while these individuals see it as part of their job and what the do every day, for us though, we would be lost without them. The Mayor congratulated the award recipients and extended her thanks to Detective Superintendent Jodi Radmore for running a very tight ship, a ship which is filled with a lot of positive comradery which is great to see.

599/2025 Resolved:

THAT Council:


  1. Receive and note the report on the NSW Government’s Environmental Planning and Assessment (Planning System Reforms) Bill (the Bill) 2025 to the Council meeting of 27 October 2025 (the Staff Report).

  2. Expresses deep concerns that the Bill reduces community participation in planning processes, undermines the role of local government and weakens existing environmental safeguards.

  3. Requests the General Manager prepares correspondence detailing Council’s concerns about the Bill (as outlined in the Staff Report) and forwards this correspondence:

  1. to our local State and Federal Members of Parliament (with a copy to all Members of the NSW Upper House); and

  2. to Local Government NSW, which includes an added request that an urgent Board Motion opposing the Bill be brought to the upcoming LGNSW Annual Conference.


The Motion was put and Carried.

Note:
In accordance with Council's Code of Meeting Practice a Division of votes is recorded on this matter.

Councillor Carmichael asking:

Why does it feel like every public square, interchange and commercial shopping centre across the greater Sydney basin seem to have broken escalators?
 
It is a regular situation at Westfield Bondi Junction.  Central Park in Broadway had two out on Saturday evening.  Central Station had two being replaced.  Westfield Parramatta and Warringah Mall recently had several out.
 
If any escalators should fail in Kiaora Lands Double Bay, is this something we should anticipate being more than a momentary matter to resolve?

Manager Property & Projects in response:

The disruptions currently affecting lifts and escalators across Sydney are due to industrial action involving Schindler, the company responsible for maintaining these systems. Schindler has informed us that ongoing service interruptions are a result of enterprise bargaining agreement (EBA) negotiations with unions. Since 6 August, technicians have implemented an indefinite ban on the use of essential tools, significantly impacting service delivery.

At our Kiaora site, an escalator in the library building is currently out of service and awaiting parts from overseas. Our Centre Manager has been in regular contact with Schindler and has been advised that installation will proceed shortly after the parts arrive in Sydney. Attempts to engage alternative service providers have been unsuccessful, as they are unwilling to work on equipment maintained by another company and would face challenges sourcing compatible parts.

Councillor Price asking:

I refer to the petition tabled at the Council meeting of 24 March 2025, initiated by Ms Wendy Coombes via change.org requesting Council to install explicit anti-littering signage and where possible, hook and line disposal bins in Yarranabbe Park, Rushcutters Bay Park and other harbourside parks. 

The petition has now received 1,047 signatures, reflecting growing community concern about the public safety risks posed by discarded fishing tackle and hooks in these areas.
I note that a sign was recently installed at the jetty at Yarranabbe Park.

Question:

Can the Director please provide an update on actions taken or planned in response to this petition, including any discussions with the Department of Primary Industries regarding educational signage, the installation of hook and line disposal bins and any other initiatives.

Manager Open Space and Trees in response:

Council staff acknowledge the impact that discarded fishing hooks and line can have and while this is not a widespread issue within the Woollahra LGA, we are working with the NSW Department of Primary Industries to install educational signage at prominent fishing locations in our area. We have installed a sign at the Yarranabbe Wharf which was a hot spot for fishing litter. 
 
In regards to the hook and line litter bins, we have previously trialled these at other locations including Parsley Bay and McKell Park. They ended up creating a bigger litter problem rather than reducing it. Despite the small opening and clear signage on the bins, they were generally filled with coffee cups, cans and other similar items. Fishing line ended up on the ground or hanging out of the bin and litter accumulated in the area. From seeing similar bins in high visitation areas this problem is common. Our experience is that they usually only work where there are mostly fishers only, no shops nearby and not many general public. 

Further educational signage will be rolled out at Parsley Bay and Rose Bay (Lyne Park).

Councillor Price asking:

To the Director of Infrastructure and Sustainability.

I refer to Council's 2025/26 Capital Works Budget and in particular, the Rushcutters Bay Catchment area works at Cecil Street, Paddington (in the amount of $1.48 million).

Can the Director please update the community on the progress of these works, including the preparation of the Review of Environmental Factors report and the likely timing of the public exhibition process.

Director Infrastructure & Sustainability in response:

The Review of Environmental Factors for the project, which incorporates updated flood modelling reflecting recent flood mitigation works in the catchment, has been completed and undergone review by Council’s Director Planning and Place. The outcome of that review is that further information has been requested relating to contamination status of soils in Trumper Park. This is a material issue as the status of the soils may affect the planning and approvals pathway for the project, i.e. there may be a requirement to undergo a DA process rather approval under the Infrastructure SEPP. This matter remains under consideration. 

 

Further to these considerations, the Director Infrastructure and Sustainability has requested the Manager Engineering Services and the project team to review again the justification for the project. In asking for this further review, the Director has had particular regard to recent rain events e.g. September 10, 2025. During this event and others in recent years, there has been flooding in surrounding suburbs and at other sites in Paddington, but no property inundation has been reported in Cecil Street. This suggests the possibility that other works in the catchment, particularly the recent works by Council and Sydney Water in adjacent Hampden Street, have been more effective in managing the issues in Cecil Street than the updated modelling suggests. Noting the significant cost of the project, the potential impact on Trumper Park and the relatively small number of properties that will benefit, the Director is seeking greater certainty around justification before proceeding to reporting to Council and consulting with the broader community.

 

The first step in the review will be direct contact with residents in Cecil Street and neighbouring streets to ‘ground truth’ the results of the updated modelling. This work will commence in the coming weeks.

(Councillor Dixson/Councillor Robertson)

624/2025 Resolved without debate:


THAT Council:

  1. Endorse that overdue fines are no longer charged at Woollahra Libraries from 1 December 2025. 

  2. Note that a new ‘support to comply’ model that uses restrictions on library membership as a compliance lever will be implemented from 1 December 2025.

  3. Note that the discontinuation of library fines from 1 December 2025 would result in a reduction in budgeted income for 2025-2026 of approximately $25,300 and a budget adjustment to reflect this would be included in Council's second quarter budget review process. 

The Motion was put and Carried.

Note:
In accordance with Council's Code of Meeting Practice a Division of votes is recorded on this matter.

634/2025 Recommendation:

THAT Council:

  1. Notes the ‘Preliminary heritage assessment of Darling Point places’ prepared by Council’s Senior Strategic Heritage Officer at Attachment 1 of the report to the Environmental Planning Committee of 3 November 2025.

  2. Supports the further investigation of the identified seven buildings as part of existing or future studies as identified in the Heritage Gap Analysis, in line with existing priorities established in the Heritage Gap Analysis.

  3. Requests staff to investigate the significance of historical public works in the municipality, including in Darling Point, subject to the investigation being identified as a low priority under the Heritage Gap Analysis.

  4. Supports investigations into the view corridor and trees of significance along the driveway of 13 Eastbourne Road as a ‘significant vista’, in the Darling Point Precinct, which could form part of a future proposed amendment to the Woollahra Development Control Plan 2015.

  5. Requests staff investigate the Phoenix palm (adjacent to 13 Eastbourne Road) as shown in figure 11 of the report for listing on Council’s Significant Tree Register. 

  6. Expresses its thanks and appreciation to the Darling Point Society for their contribution to the ‘Preliminary heritage assessment of Darling Point places’ and their longstanding commitment to the preservation of Darling Point’s heritage. 

The Motion was put and Carried.

 

Note:
In accordance with Council's Code of Meeting Practice a Division of votes is recorded on this matter.

For the MotionAgainst the Motion

635/2025 Recommendation:

THAT Council:

  1. Resolves to repeal the Woollahra Section 94 Contributions Plan 2002 as contained at Attachment 1 of the report to the Environmental Planning Committee of 3 November 2025.

  2. Notes that as at 30 September 2025, Council held an unspent balance of $1,146,882 under the Woollahra Section 94 Contributions Plan 2002 and that the allocation of these unspent funds should be as follows:

Note:Late correspondence was tabled by Yvonne & Daniel Wise, John Ralston, Weir Phillips Heritage, SJB Planning, McKees, GBA Heritage and Mr & Mrs Smith.

Note:Lauren Schutz, Hamish Halley, Patrick Holland, Annette English and Jessica Walsh, Objectors and James Phillips and Alice Fuller on behalf of 8 Glencoe Road, Heritage Consultant addressed the Panel.

Panel's Decision


THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel advises Council to proceed with the Planning 

Proposal (at Attachment 1) to list the following three (3) buildings and one (1) HCA on the 

associated Heritage Maps of the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014:


  1. ‘House and interiors’ at 50 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot B DP 330100)
  2. ‘House’ at 58 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 5 DP 15520) 
  3. ‘House’ at 8 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 4 DP 17153)
  4. The ‘Glencoe Estate HCA’, consisting of eleven (11) buildings:
  1. 2 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot A DP 330100)
  2. 3 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lots 0-3 SP 22439)
  3. 4 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 9 DP 15520)
  4. 5 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 8 DP: 15520)
  5. 6 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 7 DP 17153)
  6. 7 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 6A DP 17153)
  7. 8 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 4 DP 17153)
  8. 50 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot B DP 330100)
  9. 56 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 3 DP 17153)
  10. 58 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 5 DP 15520)
  11. 60 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 6 DP 17153)

 

Reasons

The Panel conducted site inspections and appreciates the time of the residents in making 

their written and oral submissions. 

 

The Panel notes the representations in relation to the impact and timing of recent State led 

Planning Initiatives. However, this should not prevent or preclude Council from progressing 

its adopted heritage programme which was planned and budgeted following the adoption by

Council of the Heritage Gap Analysis on 22 November 2021.    

 

The Woollahra LPP advises Council that the Planning Proposal has strategic and site-

specific merit, for the following reasons:


  • That the properties individually and collectively contribute to the understanding of the history and the heritage of the municipality
  • That the level of research and investigation combined with the attention to detail to analyse and assess various issues during the listing process has been robust and comprehensive
  • That the pre-engagement with the affected parties has been well-considered and enhanced the listing process
  • That this is the very early stage of the heritage process, and there will be multiple opportunities for owners to provide feedback should the proposed heritage listings progress
  • That, following the site inspection by the members of the panel, advice from Council’s heritage staff and consultant, and submissions, the interiors of 58 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra should not be included as part of the heritage item’s listing. 

Note: In accordance with the Woollahra Local Planning Panel Operational Procedures the votes are recorded on this planning matter.

For the MotionAgainst the Motion

Luise Elsing
Penelope Holloway
Kerry Kyriacou


4/0

Panel’s Decision

THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, refuse development consent to Development Application No. 235/2025/1 for the demolition of the existing strata-titled building and construction of new residential flat building including affordable housing, associated landscaping and strata subdivision on land at 365 Edgecliff Road EDGECLIFF.

Panel’s Decision
 
THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, is satisfied that the matters required to be addressed under Clause 4.6(3) of the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014 have been demonstrated and that consent may be granted to the development application, which contravenes the Floor Space Ratio development standard under Clauses 4.4E of Woollahra LEP 2014.
 
AND
 
THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, grant development consent to DA245/2025/1 for Alterations and additions to the existing dwelling including removal of trees on land at 10 Edward Street WOOLLAHRA, subject to the recommended conditions.
 
Reasons for Decision
 
The Panel has undertaken a site orientation, considered submissions, late correspondence  and reviewed the assessment report prepared by Council officers that addresses the relevant matters detailed in Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act
1979.
 
The Panel in considering the late correspondence decided to delete Conditions D.1 c) (Roof Profile) and d) (Materiality of Openings) on the grounds that it would not diminish the heritage significance of the development within a HCA.
 
For the reasons generally in the assessment report, the Panel is satisfied that the application can be approved subject to the Conditions as set out in the Attachment (Adopted Conditions of Consent).

 


Note: In accordance with the Woollahra Local Planning Panel Operational Procedures the votes are recorded on this planning matter.

For the MotionAgainst the Motion


Judith ClarkNil
Luise Elsing
Penelope Holloway
Kerry Kyriacou


4/0

Panel’s Decision


THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council as the consent authority, is satisfied that the matters required to be addressed under Clause 4.6(3) of the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014 have been demonstrated and that consent may be granted to the development application, which contravenes Clause 4.3 Height of Buildings and Clause 4.4E Floor Space Ratio development standards under the Woollahra LEP 2014. 


AND


THAT the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, exercising the functions of Council, as the consent authority, grant development consent to DA343/2025/1 for alterations and additions to an approved new dwelling on land at 22 Cooper Street DOUBLE BAY, subject to the recommended conditions in Attachment 2.


Reasons for Decision

The Panel has undertaken site inspection, considered the submissions, and reviewed the assessment report prepared by Council officers that addresses the relevant matters detailed in Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.  

For the reasons generally in the assessment report, the Panel is satisfied that the application can be approved subject to the Conditions as set out in Attachment (Adopted Conditions of Consent).

Note: In accordance with the Woollahra Local Planning Panel Operational Procedures the votes are recorded on this planning matter.

For the Motion
Against the Motion

Helen Lochhead
Isabelle Shapiro

Reasons for Decision

The Panel has undertaken site inspection, considered the submissions, and reviewed the assessment report prepared by Council officers that addresses the relevant matters detailed in Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.  

For the reasons generally in the assessment report, the Panel is satisfied that the application can be approved subject to the Conditions as set out in Attachment (Adopted Conditions of Consent).

Note: In accordance with the Woollahra Local Planning Panel Operational Procedures the votes are recorded on this planning matter.

Note: In accordance with Clause 18.2 of Council's Code of Meeting Practice, the Council extended the time of the meeting by 5 minutes.

Note: Councillor Ardouin, Councillor Mitchell, Councillor Robertson and Councillor Zeltzer left the meeting during this item, the time being 10:25pm.

 

Councillor Price:

  • Local Government NSW Conference 

Councillor Price advised that she, along with Councillor Regan, Councillor Witt, Councillor Mitchell, the Mayor, and the General Manager, recently attended the Local Government NSW Conference at Penrith Panthers. She extended her thanks to Patricia Vella (Executive Assistant to the Mayor/General Manager), for facilitating the Councillor's attendance at the conference. Councillor Price noted that it was an excellent conference, praising Councillor Witt's points raised at the conference regarding State Government reforms, which were well-received by fellow Councillors.

Councillor Witt:

  • Critical Path

Councillor Witt advised that she recently attended the 20th year celebration of 'Critical Path'. Councillor Witt stated that it was a wonderful insight into the creative process, and a reminder of why performing arts is so important. Councillor Witt highlighted the invaluable role that Woollahra Council plays in supporting this organisation. Councillor Witt reported on a documentary titled 'Breakthroughs', presented by Deborah May and an insightful speech by Virginia Leonard, the winner of the Woollahra Small Sculpture Prize.

Councillor Parmegiani:

  • Local Government NSW Conference

Councillor Parmegiani provided an update from his attendance at the Local Government NSW Conference. Councillor Parmegiani noted several points from the conference in that many NSW Council's are facing financial difficulties, rural Councils are currently divided over the issue of renewable energy, and the Conference heard from a marketing expert who provided commentary on the differences between public exhibitions and properly conducted market research.

Councillor Jarvis:

  • Doing Business in Woollahra
  • Supporting Charities
  • Remembrance Day 2025 - November 9 & 11
  • Melbourne Cup luncheon at Easts, Rose Bay 
  • Sculpture Walk One Artwork Closer

Councillor Jarvis sends her congratulations to the staff for organising yet another successful Doing Business in Woollahra Networking evening held at the Woollahra Library on October 29 and extends her thanks to all those small business owners who attended. Representing the Mayor, Councillor Jarvis made the official welcome before they heard from a Small Business Month panel of retailers who shared their experience most notably Mary Read, owner of 'Reads' who has now successfully operated her boutique in Queen Street for over 30 years. Retail consultant Kevin Hannah spoke about energising our retail sector and sharing practical strategies to help businesses thrive. Eg creating ‘wow’ in a retail shop window. Also present was the General Manager, Director of Planning and Place Scott Pedder, Strategic Planning and Place Manager Anne White, Economic Development Coordinator James Granter as well as Councillors Hugh Woodgate and Alexander Andruska. With over 10,000 businesses in Woollahra we are all proud to initiative and support these networking nights. 

 

October 31 2025 saw an invitation to the Mayor for the Making Waves Regatta. Councillor Jarvis attended on her behalf and went out on the harbour with an excellent crew of 'Shine On' with 'Making Waves' who told her about the great work of 'Making Waves' in making sailing accessible for those who are not so able bodied, some of who even go on to compete in the Sydney to Hobart Race and will participate this Boxing Day. It happens that 'Making Waves' is a tenant of the Council at the Drill Hall and hope we can find them more accessible accommodation. 

Councillor Jarvis congratulates members of the Rose Bay RSL Sub-Branch, President Charles Gallagher and Secretary Beverley Bruen, Alan and Rosemary Stockley OAM who organised another moving ceremony, flag raising and wreath laying ceremony of November 11. Councillor Jarvis laid a wreath on behalf of the Mayor. Also in attendance was Commanding Officer Kathryn Jones of HMAS Watson, Councillor Torsten, Lorraine Emerson, President of the Garden Clubs of Australia, and Mrs Chrissie Hughes. The National Anthem was sung by Ms Cosgrove who has a quite exceptional voice. This followed an earlier ceremony at the NSW Association of Jewish Service Ex-Service Men and Women (NAJEX) for the communal wreath laying and Remembrance Day Service on November 9 . Held at the National Council of Jewish Women Australia we were welcomed by Roger Selby who announced that he stepping down as NAJEX President after decades of service. Councillor Jarvis congratulates and thanks Roger Selby for his service. Those in attendance included Rabbi Mendel Kastel OAM and Rabbi Dr Dovid Rabbi Slavo, and other leaders of the Jewish community.  Also in attendance was Minister for Local Government Hon Ron Hoenig MP, Scott Farlow, Susan Carter MLC and Councillor Woodgate from Woollahra Council.

Councillor Jarvis advised that it was wonderful to see local girls, originally from Melbourne, organise yet another marvellous ladies luncheon at Easts, Rose Bay. Most of the 40 women who joined them also now live in the Woollahra Council area. The food was delicious and champagne flowed freely especially for the winners of multiple sweeps, where other locals also gathered to witness Jamie Melham on 'Half Yours', only the second woman to ride the Melbourne Cup winner. 

Finally, the Woollahra Public Art Panel chaired by Councillor Zeltzer met on November 12, and Councillor Jarvis was particularly excited to have further reports on the installation of 'Quantum', a gift from from former Redleaf local Ron Robertson Swann OAM who has gone onto become one of the greatest living Australian Sculptors, and was honoured with a special invitation to instal one of his works at this years 'Sculptures by the Sea'. The hope of Councillor Parmegiani and Councillor Jarvis is to see a permanent exhibition installed along the Christison Park and Lighthouse Reserve walk is one step closer to being realised.


Councillor Carmichael:

  • Jewish International Film Festival 

Councillor Carmichael reported that he recently attended the Jewish International Film Festival. He advised that Council had provided assistance to two film directors who approached Council regarding the events of 7 October 2023 and subsequent incidents within the Woollahra LGA. Councillor Carmichael noted that the film was very moving, and acknowledged that both Woollahra Council and Councillor Carmichael were mentioned in the credits. He expressed his appreciation to Council for supporting these filmmakers, highlighting that few organisations are currently offering assistance to Jewish filmmakers.


Councillor Torsten:

  • Head On Festival
  • Remembrance Day Service
  • Congratulations to Kellie Sloane MP

Councillor Torsten advised that he recently attended the Head On Festival, and congratulated Moshe Rosenveig and Anita Schwartz for holding the successful 16th Head On Photo Festival.

 

Councillor Torsten suggested that Woollahra Gallery explore opportunities to host a Head On exhibition in the future.

Councillor Torsten, along with Councillor Jarvis attended the Rose Bay RSL Remembrance Day Service and congratulated the Rose Bay Sub-Branch on hosting the service. Councillor Torsten expressed that the service in an important we pay our respects to those that sacrificed so much.

Councillor Torsten congratulated Kellie Sloane MP on her appointment as Leader of the Opposition, NSW. 


Councillor Andruska:

  • International Men's Day
  • Doing Business in Woollahra

On 19 November 2025, Councillor Andruska along with Councillor Mitchell and Councillor Carmichael, attended a 'Lifeline' event held in Bondi to raise money for International Men's Day.

Councillor Andruska reported that he attended the 'Doing Business in Woollahra' event, and praised Councillor Jarvis for her presentation at the event.


The Mayor, Councillor Dixson:

  • Local Government NSW Conference
  • Celebrate Double Bay Event
  • School End of Year Celebrations
  • Roundtable of Liberal Mayors and Shadow Ministers
  • Opening of Royal Motor Yacht Club Sailing Season
  • Puppy Cup 2025 
  • Jewish House – Gala Dinner
  • Remembrance Day Commemoration Ceremony

From the 23 to 25 November 2025, The Mayor, Councillor Dixson attended the Local Government NSW Conference with Councillor Price, Councillor Regan, Councillor Parmegiani, Councillor Witt, and Councillor Mitchell along with the General Manager, where Council was successful with its submitted Motions. The Mayor wished to congratulate Inner West Mayor, Councillor Darcy Byrne who was elected President of Local Government NSW for the next two years.

On 30 October 2025, Council launched the 'Celebrate Double Bay Event'. The Mayor expressed that it is shaping up to be a great week in February 2026, and reminds everyone to have 21 and 22 February 2026 in your diaries.

The Mayor expresses her thanks to all the Councillors who are stepping in to attend all these School End of Year Celebrations for 2025.

On 30 October 2025, the Mayor attended the 'Roundtable of Liberal Mayors and Shadow Ministers', where attendees discussed issues facing Local Government.

On 1 November 2025, the Mayor attended the opening of Royal Motor Yacht Club Sailing Season.

On 1 November 2025, the Mayor attended 'Puppy Cup 2025', and enjoyed attending this Grant Recipient Event.

On 6 November 2025, the Mayor attended the Jewish House Gala Dinner. The Mayor was pleased to attend this evening with her family.

On 9 November 2025, the Mayor attended the Remembrance Day Commemoration Ceremony hosted by the Paddington Woollahra RSL Sub-Branch. The Mayor was honoured to lay a Wreath on behalf of Council and the Woollahra Community for Remembrance Day 11 November 2025.

675/2025 Resolved:

THAT Council:

  1. Notes the ‘Preliminary heritage assessment of Darling Point places’ prepared by Council’s Senior Strategic Heritage Officer at Attachment 1 of the report to the Environmental Planning Committee of 3 November 2025.

  2. Supports the further investigation of the identified seven buildings as part of existing or future studies as identified in the Heritage Gap Analysis, in line with existing priorities established in the Heritage Gap Analysis.

Councillor Silcocks asking:

Noting the NSW Planning Minister’s latest public comments regarding LMR reforms: “It was Woollahra Council which zoned that land [low lying areas of Double Bay and Rose Bay] as appropriate for low and medium density housing and as the consent authority on development applications they have the responsibility to assess suitable and safe development on that land………Government is not considering exemptions to the policy but always encourages councils to undertake their own strategic planning that will deliver more homes.” (Sydney Morning Herald 3rd November 2025).

  1. When Council zoned “that land” for low and medium density, what were the height, bulk and FSR controls and was there any expectation that “medium density’ would extend to 8 storey apartment blocks with no minimum lot size and with parking requirements necessitating two levels of excavation?

  2. Is Council still the “consent authority?”

  3. Does Council have ultimate responsibility for assessing “suitable and safe” development?
  1. Must other planning authorities (Planning Panels, L&E, HAD etc) defer to Council’s assessment when it comes to safety and suitability?

 

  1. Rather than “exemptions” per se, does this confirm that Council has the opportunity to propose its own “strategic planning” solutions to “deliver more homes” (e.g. Edgecliff Commercial Centre Planning and Urban Design Strategy), which would effectively obviate the need for the LMR policy?
  1. Noting that Council’s current 2029 target is 1,900 new dwellings.
  2. But that the LMR is open ended and unaligned to any particular target.
  3. So what is the actual WMC housing target?

  1. Further noting additional comments by a spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure that: “Individual councils are able to consider impacts to local character as part of the development assessment process.” (Wentworth Courier 5th November 2025).
  1. Does this add further weight to Council’s DCP?
  2. Does this empower Council to argue that 6-8 storey apartment blocks are unacceptably disruptive to the “local character” of 1 to 3 storey residential streets?’ 

Manager Strategic Planning & Place in response:

  1. When Council zoned “that land” for low and medium density, what were the height, bulk and FSR controls and was there any expectation that “medium density’ would extend to 8 storey apartment blocks with no minimum lot size and with parking requirements necessitating two levels of excavation? 

It has never been Council’s intention that development of 6 storeys or more would be permitted on residentially zoned land around the Double Bay and Rose Bay Centres, which is now the subject of the State Government’s Low and Mid-Rise Housing Policy (LMR).
 
Under the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014(Woollahra LEP 2014), a maximum height of buildings of 9.5 to 10.5m applies to most land zoned R3 Medium Density Residential.

A corresponding floor space ratio (FSR) of between 0.65:1 to 1:1 then applies on most sites. These controls provide for development of up to 3 storeys.
 
The current Woollahra LEP 2014 controls are consistent with the controls in Council’s previous Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 1995  (which was repealed on 23 May 2015). In 2012 – 2013 staff undertook a comprehensive review of the height and FSR controls that apply around the Double Bay and Rose Bay Centres, and Council resolved to make minimal changes to the maximum building heights and maximum FSR controls that apply in these areas.
 
Furthermore, these height and FSR controls are supported by the Woollahra Development Control Plan 2015 (Woollahra DCP 2015), which establishes the desired future character for these residential precincts, and there has never been any expectation in Council’s planning framework that residential density would extend to 8 storey development. 

2. Is Council still the “consent authority?”

 The consent authority is determined by the scale and value of the development application (DA).

  • Council is the consent authority for development that is local development. Development is considered local development if a local environmental plan (LEP) or State environmental planning policy (SEPP) states that development consent is required before the development can take place, and the development is not Regionally Significant Development or State Significant Development. 



    The General Manager has delegations to determine development applications (DAs), which are then sub-delegated to relevant staff including the Application Assessment Panel, the Director Planning and Place, the Manager Development Assessment and the Development Assessment Team Leaders. 

    Applications of a more complex nature are reported to the Woollahra Local Planning Panel (WLPP). The principal function of the WLPP is to determine local development applications that fall within the following categories: conflict of interest, contentious development, departure from development standards, sensitive development.
  • The Sydney Eastern City Planning Panel is the consent authority for Regionally Significant Development (RSD) as listed in Schedule 6 of the State Environmental Planning Policy (Planning Systems) 2021. RSD includes development with a capital investment value over $30 million. For RSD, Council will notify and assess the DA but it will be determined by the Sydney Eastern City Planning Panel. However, staff note that the recent Planning Reforms Bill, once gazetted, will eventually eliminate this pathway. Such applications are likely to be assessed via the WLPP. 

  • State Significant Development applications (SSDA) are determined by the Minister for Planning, the Independent Planning Commission (IPC), or a delegate of either. State significant development (SSD) is development of a large scale, economic value or that carries potential social or environmental impacts can be deemed to have State significance. SSD is listed in Schedule 1\u202Fand\u202FSchedule 2 of the\u202FState Environmental Planning Policy (Planning Systems) 2021. 

    For the Woollahra LGA, SSD includes development for infill affordable housing where the residential component of the development has an estimated development cost of more than $75 million. For example, a SSDA has been lodged for land at 2-16 Spencer Street, Rose Bay. The SSDA is for a 9 storey residential flat building comprising 54 residential apartments, including 13 affordable housing apartments (for 15 years). 

  1. Does Council have ultimate responsibility for assessing “suitable and safe” development? 

  1. Must other planning authorities (Planning Panels, L&E, HAD etc) defer to Council’s assessment when it comes to safety and suitability?

As outlined in the response to Q2 above, the authority responsible for assessing development depends on the type of development:
 
  • for local development Council assesses and determines the DA either by an assessment officer under delegation or by the Local Planning Panel;
  • for regionally significant development (RSD), Council prepares an assessment report and refers it to the planning panel for determination; and 
  • for State Significant Development, the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI), prepares a report with recommendations for the Planning Minster or IPC. The DPHI consults with Council, and Council staff may make a submission for consideration. 

For local development and RSD Council is responsible for assessing the DA in accordance with section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 (EP&A Act). The assessment must have regard to all the relevant development rules (SEPPs, LEPs, and DCPs), the likely environmental impacts of the development, matters raised in submissions, and whether or not the DA is in the public interest. Council’s assessments are also informed and guided by the Planning Principles published by the Land and Environment Court. 

 

The applicant must submit a Statement of Environmental Effects (SEE) with a DA. The SEE is to address the likely impacts of the development, and the steps taken to lessen the expected impacts or to protect the environment. The SEE will often include supporting information and studies (such as a Flood Risk Management Report) prepared by suitably qualified practitioners. If the SEE does not adequately address certain matters, Council staff may ask the applicant to provide additional information or studies. 
 
The owner’s consent in lodging the DA includes a declaration “that all the information given is true and correct”. It is an offence to provide false or misleading information. Development consent that is based on that false information can be found void if challenged, and the applicant can be prosecuted for providing that false and misleading information. 
 
Where Council has properly assessed and considered the impacts of the development having regard to the EP&A Act, the SEE, issues raised in submissions and any other advice and referrals, Council has acted in good faith and is protected from liability.

  1. Rather than “exemptions” per se, does this confirm that Council has the opportunity to propose its own “strategic planning” solutions to “deliver more homes” (e.g. Edgecliff Commercial Centre Planning and Urban Design Strategy), which would effectively obviate the need for the LMR policy?
  1. Noting that Council’s current 2029 target is 1,900 new dwellings.
  2. But that the LMR is open ended and unaligned to any particular target.
  3. So what is the actual WMC housing target?

The State Government did not provide WMC with an opportunity to provide alternate solutions to the LMR to deliver more housing.

The DPHI has not issued councils with revised housing targets. More broadly, the NSW Government has committed to building 377,000 new homes across the state in the next 5 years to align with the National Housing Accord, and it is expected that the Low and Mid-Rise policy will deliver 112,000 homes over the next 5 years. It is further noted that the NSW Premier announced on 24 August 2025 that the proposed rezoning around the existing Edgecliff and the proposed Woollahra train stations would enable up to 10,000 new homes in the Woollahra LGA.
 
Staff were informed that the State Government would release a Draft Metropolitan Plan and supporting District Plans by the end of 2025.  This would replace the Eastern City District Plan which was adopted in 2018.  Staff anticipate that new housing targets would be contained in the relevant District Plan. 

  1. Further noting additional comments by a spokesperson for the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure that: “Individual councils are able to consider impacts to local character as part of the development assessment process.” (Wentworth Courier 5th November 2025) 
  1. Does this add further weight to Council’s DCP?
  2. Does this empower Council to argue that 6-8 storey apartment blocks are unacceptably disruptive to the “local character” of 1 to 3 storey residential streets?’ 
The LMR sets out non-discretionary development standards, also known as non-refusal standards. For example, the new standards for residential flat buildings that will apply in LMR areas in the R3 Medium Density Residential zone within the Woollahra LGA are:
 
  • Floor space ratio: max 2.2:1
  • Height of building: max 22m for residential flat buildings and 24m for a building containing shop top housing
  • Storeys: max 6
  • No minimum lot size or width 

 

These non-discretionary standards prevail over an equivalent standard in the Woollahra LEP 2014 or Woollahra DCP 2015 that is more onerous. The consent authority therefore cannot refuse a DA which complies with the non-discretionary standards on the basis of non-compliance with Council’s LEP or DCP. 
 
A merit assessment of the applications will still be undertaken, and the Woollahra LEP 2014 and Woollahra DCP 2015 will still apply to development, but only to matters not covered by the non-discretionary standards in the Housing SEPP. The local character as identified in the Woollahra DCP 2015 will be considered in the assessment, and balanced by the consent authority when considering the proposal. However, the controls contained in the Woollahra DCP 2015 must be applied flexibly under s4.15(3A) of the EP&A Act.

Councillor Carmichael asking:

A resident has approached me asking for Council to review the green pedestrian light signalling for this smaller left turn lane into New South Head Road Double Bay from William Street.  The resident argues the time is much too short for reasonably walking across.

Could Council staff please kindly examine this request and, if staff support the claim, advocate to TfNSW through the appropriate channels to improve signal timing here?


Manager Engineering Services in response:

Council staff have undertaken a preliminary investigation on this matter, which identifies that the current length of pedestrian green light cycle may be too short for the crossing distance. This matter will be referred to TfNSW for review and consider improvement to the pedestrian signal phasing at this intersection.

Councillor Carmichael asking:

Approximately half of the Double Bay and Bellevue Road smart poles appear to be out during the evening again.  Can Council please kindly investigate/resolve?

Separately, can Council investigate a more efficient/automated means to outage detection than relying on resident or Councillor reports?  I have raised this issue before on multiple occasions over the past several years.  There needs to be a better way to ensure the lights are on.

 


Manager Engineering Service in response:

Council staff are investigating street lighting in Double Bay and have identified faulty streetlights which are either owned by Ausgrid or Council. Ausgrid’s faulty streetlights will be reported to Ausgrid directly, through their online portal. The streetlights along New South Head Road within the commercial centre are Council owned, and a contractor has been engaged to inspect and repair Council’s streetlights, where necessary. An innovative solution to see whether there is a way to inform the light is faulty has been asked of with the contractor and feedback will be provided once investigated.

Currently, there is no automated technique to detect faulty streetlights. A faulty light is identified by observation on-site by a member of the public. Ausgrid’s website contains an online portal to report faulty streetlights which can be accessed by the community and is the same process which Council staff report faulty lights to Ausgrid.

Ausgrid does not provide a fixed timeframe for completion of works and there are multiple factors, including competing electrical repairs across the State, supply of materials, nature of works, any other approval requirements ie. road occupancy licences, that may result in any delays.

Note: 
Late correspondence was tabled by Councillor Harriet Price. Esther Hayter (The Paddington Society), and Nina Radzyminski.

(Councillor Price/Councillor Robertson)

694/2025 Resolved:

THAT Council:

  1. Notes:

     The Proposal

  1. A State Significant Development (SSD) has been declared for 160 Oxford Street and 142-148 Oxford Street, Paddington (the Proposal).1

  2. The Proposal seeks to demolish the existing building at 160 Oxford Street (containing 27 self-contained studio apartments) and the adjoining contemporary townhouses at 142-148 Oxford Street to construct a new eight to nine storey development (comprising 44 apartments including a 4 storey basement car park with 78 car spaces).

  3. The estimated development cost (EDC) of the Proposal is $78,300,000.

  4. Approximately 12 dwellings are proposed to be designated as 'affordable housing', resulting in a net loss of approximately 15 affordable dwellings.

  5. A ground floor retail development is mentioned on the Proponent’s website but is not contained in the Proposal.2

    Council’s Planning and Heritage Strategies and Policies

  1. Goal 1 of its ‘Community Strategic Plan’ to:
    ‘Encourage and facilitate high-quality planning and urban design outcomes and spaces’.3

  2. Planning Priority 5 of its ‘Woollahra Local Strategic Planning Statement’ (the LSP Statement):
    ‘Conserving our rich and diverse heritage’.4

  3. Action Item 28 from the LSP Statement to:
    'Continue to proactively conserve and monitor heritage in the Municipality’.5

  4. Its endorsement of the ‘Heritage GAP Analysis’ in November 2021 and in particular, the ongoing action to:

    ‘Remain vigilant on development and threats to unlisted heritage - continue reviewing development applications and complying development certificates to minimise loss of unlisted heritage and issue Interim Heritage Orders under s25 of the New South Wales Heritage Act 1977.

    Ensure there are resources to undertake ad-hoc heritage assessments in the event of a threat.’6 
     Community Concerns

  1. The significant concerns of the Paddington community regarding the Proposal and in particular, the:
  1. loss of affordable housing;
  2. impacts to the Paddington Heritage Conservation Area (HCA), especially to the beautifully preserved and much loved original cottages that housed the workers that built the Barracks;
  3. traffic, excavation and amenity implications;
  4. overshadowing of the public open space on Oxford Street;
  5. impacts on Oxford Street’s jacaranda trees;
  6. lack of community consultation; and
  7. difficulties navigating the complexities of a SSD.

  1. The following information from the Paddington Society concerning 142 Oxford Street:
    ‘Number 142 is built over a disused sandstone basement which was possibly used as a cool room in the early days of the construction of the barracks. The basement   is little known and is not used as part of the dwelling above but is of extreme historical significance and requires a detailed heritage and archaeological investigation. There may be similar basements beneath the other townhouses.’7
  2. Its heritage staff have undertaken a ‘desktop’ review of the property at 160 Oxford Street and have assessed that the site would not meet the threshold for a local heritage listing.
  3. The letter from Cr Harriet Price to the Minister for Planning and Public Spaces dated 26 November 2026 requesting an extension to the exhibition period (tabled as late correspondence).

    14. The newly formed Paddington Community group ‘Paddington United’ and their Change.Org petition entitled ‘Better Development for all not Luxury for a few’ that has garnered 1072 verified signatures in less than 2 weeks. 

  1. Resolves that:

  1. The General Manager directs Council's Planning staff to:

 

  1. undertake a review of the Proposal, including but not limited to an assessment of the following issues:
  1. the Community Concerns outlined at paragraph A10 (above);
  2. the impacts to the Paddington and the State heritage listed, Victoria Barracks;
  3. the loss of genuine affordable housing, inconsistent with the objectives of the NSW Infill Affordable Housing Policy; and
  4. whether the Proposal meets the criteria of the State Environmental Planning Policy (Housing) 2021) (Housing SEPP), especially with regards to the ground floor retail component.
  1. prepare and lodge a formal submission during the exhibition period.

  1. The General Manager (or delegate) undertakes a ‘desktop’ review and investigation of the potential heritage significance (or otherwise) of the reported, disused sandstone basement located at 142 Oxford Street (and possibly beneath the adjoining townhouses).

  2. If the item referred to in paragraph B2 (above):
  1. meets the threshold for a local heritage listing, writes to the Minister responsible for the Heritage Act to make an Interim Heritage Order; and
  2. Does not meet the threshold for a local heritage listing, then advise Councillors via memorandum of this.
     
  1. The Mayor writes to:

    a. The Minister for Planning and Public Spaces requesting an extension to the exhibition period in similar terms to the letter from Cr Price referred to in paragraph A.13 (above); and

    b. Lord Mayor Clover Moore AO and Alex Greenwich MP informing them both of:

    i. the Proposal;
    ii. the Community concerns; and
    ii. this Notice of Motion.

The Motion was put and Carried.

Nina Radzyminski, Norm Hacker, Paul Cottee, Ralph Dayman, Renee Symonds, Richard Eskell & Amanda L'Estrange, Robert Goot, Robin Spiro, Roger Muller, Ros Isaacs, The Rose Bay Collaboration Team, The Rose Bay Residents Action Group, Roy Woodhouse, Sally Goodchild, Shanon Folden, Shauna Corne, Sheena Frenkel, Sheridan Hopkins, Shula Holtzman, Stephen Lewis & Leonie Symonds, Stephen Baer, Stephen Feldman, Susan Park, Susann Minbashian, Terri Solsky, Tim Hargreaves, Tom Boycott, Tony Bond, Trevor Gerber, Valerie & Allan Edwards, Wendy Baer, and Wendy Fine.

Motion moved by Councillor Witt
Seconded by Councillor Regan

That Council: 

  1. Notes that the state government has repeatedly refused Council's well-founded requests to remove the applicable R3 medium density residential zones of Rose Bay and Double Bay from the application of the Low and Mid-Rise (LMR) Housing Policy. 

  2. Notes that Council has provided the state government with persuasive information about the well documented hydrogeological and flooding hazards affecting both of these centres, and also with reports of extensive damage from excavation and flooding to existing buildings and infrastructure. 

  3. Notes that State Significant and other Development Applications (DAs) lodged since the introduction of the LMR Housing Policy in Rose Bay and Double Bay are leading to proposals for large scale and deep basement excavations far in excess of Council's existing controls. 

  4. Notes that the LMR non refusal standards for height and FSR, coupled with the application of the Affordable Housing Bonus (AHB) and the lack of a requirement for a minimum lot size in the LMR R3 medium-density zones, severely constrains the effectiveness of the various DA assessment processes (eg Council, Department of Planning Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) and/or the Land and Environment Court) to protect property owners and residents from damage to property from excavation in the hydrogeologically and geotechnically sensitive areas of Rose Bay and Double Bay.

  5. Notes that rezoning land within the Woollahra Local Government Area (LGA) is the primary mechanism for meeting the most important aim of the Woollahra Local Environment Plan (WLEP): “2(a) to ensure that growth occurs in a planned and co-ordinated way.”

  6. Requests Staff to expeditiously investigate and report back on the feasibility of rezoning land within the mapped settlement areas of Rose Bay and Double Bay from R3 Medium Density to R2 Low Density in order to reduce settlement and flooding risks in these very sensitive areas. See maps below.1

  7. Notes that given the reports of damage 100 metres or more away from excavation sites, land extending beyond the mapped settlement areas of Rose Bay and Double Bay may also need to be considered for lower density rezoning.2  

  8. Notes that the rezoning of the Rose Bay and Double Bay settlement areas for lower density is consistent with the Minister for Planning and Public Spaces, the Hon Paul Scully MP, view that councils are responsible for appropriately zoning land for low and medium density housing and “as the consent authority on development applications they have the responsibility to assess suitable and safe development on that land.”3

  9. Notes that the proposed rezoning of land from R3 Medium Density to R2 Low Density in the Rose Bay and Double Bay settlement areas does not preclude further densification of these areas, and that a significant amount of medium density housing in the applicable R3 Medium Density Residential zones has already been approved and/or built over the last 20 years.

  10. Notes that while Council is taking steps to investigate and model the cumulative impacts of excavation in the LMR R3 medium-density residential zones of Rose Bay and Double Bay, the recent influx of LMR SSDAs and DAs, the damage already observed, and the clear risk of further harm, requires Council to take a precautionary approach to minimising exposure to legal, financial, and regulatory consequences.

The Motion was put and Lost.

697/2025 Resolved:

THAT Council:

  1. Notes that the Urban Forest strategy, approved by the community and unanimously adopted by Council on November 2023 aims to increase tree canopy in our Council area to 30% within 25 years (https://www.woollahra.nsw.gov.au/files/dc033cd3-7056-43ee-a55c-4fb277a910d7/Urban-Forest-Strategy-2023.pdf).

  2. Notes ongoing reports of destruction to street trees and trees in parks, whether dying or poisoned or without Council approval, being pruned.

  3. Requests the General Manager provide a report proposing proactive measures that can be taken to address situations where trees have been impacted in those circumstances.

  4. Particular consideration is requested to be given where the destruction occurs on Council footpath verges or open spaces and in front of sites which have recently sold, have newly approved DAs or under development, the result which creates or provides a view that didn’t previously exist.

    That the following options be considered:
  • Greater use of banner signs where smaller or newly planted trees have been poisoned or damaged.
  • For larger or mature trees that have been poisoned or damaged, not only a banner but the erection of a permanent hoarding.
  • Where the tree has been or is poisoned or damaged is in front of a site of development site or recently completely development thereby creating a view that didn’t exist before it be treated as the most serious case.
  • For more serious cases, placement of a shroud over the dead tree until such time as a replacement tree is mature.
  • A larger sign to highlight that the tree has been poisoned or illegally pruned thereby obliterating any view that is created by the destruction of the trees.
  • Where a mature tree is poisoned and is dead, replacing it with a large growing species.
  • Where there is one tree that is poisoned, multiple replacements are planted nearby as part of the UFS.
  • Replanting the poisoned fig tree on New South Head Road Bellevue Hill and adding an additional fig nearby.
  • Investigate the use of CCTV near vandalised trees.
  • Community education and develop better messaging rather than the standard advice  Such as “See it, film it, report it”;  to encourage protection “Please look after this tree as the previous trees here were poisoned. If you see something, report it Council”. “Street trees are for everyone’s enjoyment. You need Council approval if you want to prune them in anyway”.
  1. Requests an advice on costs and whether they can form part of the costs of the Urban Forest Strategy. Noting that a budget allocation was in the UFS for education on the importance of tree canopy. And that an allocation for Fig Management is funded in Special Rate Variation funds.

The Motion was put and Carried.

Note:
In accordance with Council's Code of Meeting Practice a Division of votes is recorded on this matter.

Note: Late correspondence was tabled by Anthony & Elizabeth Tregoning, Bobby McCarthy, Christina Stitt-Ditfurth, The Darling Point Society, David King, Gerald Abelsohn, Katherine Grinberg, Miranda Marshall, Miriam Lewin, and Ruth Phillips.

Note: Councillor Woodgate declared a Non-Significant, Non-Pecuniary Interest in this item, as the report contains evaluations conducted by Councillor Woodgate's employer, CBRE. Councillor Woodgate indicated that the department that provided certain reports functions as a separate business unit within CBRE from the one that employs Councillor Woodgate. Councillor Woodgate remained in the meeting, participated in debate and voted on the matter.

Note: Councillor Carmichael declared a Non-Significant, Non-Pecuniary Interest in this item, as the father of a close friend of Councillor Carmichael was previously a senior member of CBRE, being the company that provided the evaluations to Council. Councillor Carmichael remained in the meeting, participated in debate and voted on the matter.

Note: 
The Council meeting was adjourned at 8:32pm for 10 minutes.


Motion moved by Councillor Dixson
Seconded by Councillor Robertson

THAT Council:

  1. Notes the additional analysis on the minimum costs involved in retaining and remediating the Cross Street Car Park (Attachment 3) which would be approximately $25.6 million to $39.6 million.

  2. Notes the commentary in the report addressing other Council requests from the 24 February 2025 Council resolution.

  3. Notes the additional built form and feasibility analysis on Option 6, Option 7 and Option 8 as provided in Attachment 4 and Attachment 5 (confidential).

  4. Resolves to proceed with Option 8 (standalone carpark with subdivision and sale, which has a minimum of 412 car parking spaces) as the preferred option for the future redevelopment of the site because:

    1. It delivers a new carpark with a building life greater than any remediation option;
    2. The timeline to construct is the same as the timeline to remediate.
    3. This option has the potential to deliver affordable housing and a new community space, owned by the Council.
    4. This option does not require a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) arrangement.
    5. Any surplus funds from the sale of land will be reinvested into the community. 
    6. This option will not require a special rate variation or loan to fund the works and will maintain the financial stability of the Council.

  5. Provides owners’ consent for the General Manager (or delegate) to lodge a development application (DA) to subdivide the site to allow for the future sale of the 1,465sqm southern parcel. This DA will not include any physical works and can lapse if not required.

  6. Authorises the General Manager (or delegate) to seek tenders for the sale of the 1,465sqm southern parcel under Section 55 of the Local Government Act 1993, as follows:

    1. Sale of the parcel with a requirement for 15% of all residential floor space to be provided as affordable housing in perpetuity and 250sqm of floor space for community uses, and/or 
    2. Sale of the parcel with no requirement to provide affordable housing or community floor space to Council.

  7. Notes that further reports will be brought to Council regarding the recommended Option 8 as it progresses. These reports will address matters including;

    1. The outcome of the tender process for the sale of land, requiring decision on whether to sell, and what conditions will be applied to the sale.
    2. Granting of landowner consent for the lodgement of a DA for the new Council owned car park. Report to detail design considerations including:
      1. Maximising carparking numbers.
      2. Potential for activating the Jamberoo Lane frontage.
      3. Other design elements.
    3. Following determination of that DA, the outcome of tenders for the construction of the new Council owned car park.
    4. Temporary car parking during the construction of the new car park.
    5. Leasing and operational arrangements for the 250sqm of community space.
    6. Management arrangements for any future affordable housing component.

  8. Requests that the Mayor and General Manager (or delegate) implement a communications strategy to advise the community of this decision.

Note: 
Late correspondence was tabled by C Smith, Yvonne & Daniel Wise, Hamish Halley, Kate Cannon, and Weir Phillips Heritage.

Note: 
Jessica Baird-Walsh, Kim Chan, Hamish Halley, Daniel Wise, James Phillips, and C Smith addressed the Committee.

Note: 
Councillor Regan declared a Non-Significant, Non-Pecuniary Interest in this item, as Councillor Regan knows one of the Directors of Weir Phillips Heritage who made submissions to Council. Councillor Regan remained in the meeting, participated in debate and voted on the matter.

Note: 
Councillor Parmegiani declared a Non-Significant, Non-Pecuniary Interest in this item, as Councillor Parmegiani recently visited the 'Glencoe Estate' and spoke with a number residents of the Estate. Councillor Parmegiani remained in the meeting, participated in debate and voted on the matter.

Note: 
Councillor Torsten declared a Non-Significant, Non-Pecuniary Interest in this item, as Councillor Torsten recently visited a number of properties on Wallaroy Road and Glencoe Road, Woollahra and spoke with a number residents. Councillor Torsten remained in the meeting, participated in debate and voted on the matter.

Note: 
Councillor Jarvis declared a Non-Significant, Non-Pecuniary Interest in this item, as Councillor Jarvis is both personally and professionally associated with a number of residents of Wallaroy Road and Glencoe Road, Woollahra. Councillor Jarvis remained in the meeting, participated in debate but as a non-voting Committee member, did not vote on the matter.

Motion moved by Councillor Carmichael
Seconded by Councillor Parmegiani

THAT Council:

  1. Note the advice provided by the Woollahra Local Planning Panel on 6 November 2025 regarding the planning proposal to list three (3) buildings and one (1) Heritage Conservation Area (HCA) as local heritage items.

  2. Congratulates staff and Council’s consultant on a well justified planning proposal which was supported by a thorough heritage study which was well received by the Woollahra Local Planning Panel, where they noted “That the level of research and investigation combined with the attention to detail to analyse and assess various issues during the listing process has been robust and comprehensive”.


  3. Notes that the Glencoe Road, Woollahra Heritage Study occurred as a result of the Woollahra Heritage Gap Analysis endorsed by Council in 2021, years before the State led planning reforms were initiated. 

  4. Not withstanding the above, take no further action to progress these listings, or the heritage conservation area be taken at this time.

Amendment moved by Councillor Robertson
Seconded by Councillor Witt

THAT Council: 

 

  1. Note the advice provided by the Woollahra Local Planning Panel on 6 November 2025 regarding the planning proposal to list three (3) buildings and one (1) Heritage Conservation Area (HCA) as local heritage items.

 

  1. Endorse the Planning Proposal as contained at Attachment 1 of the report to the Environmental Planning Committee of 1 December 2025 to list the following three (3) buildings and one (1) HCA in Schedule 5 and on the associated Heritage Maps of the Woollahra Local Environmental Plan 2014: 


  1. ‘House' at 50 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot B DP 330100) 
  2. ‘House’ at 58 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 5 DP 15520) 
  3. ‘House’ at 8 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 4 DP 17153) 
  4. The ‘Glencoe Estate HCA’, consisting of eleven (11) buildings:  
  1. 2 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot A DP 330100)
  2. 3 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lots 0-3 SP 22439)
  3. 4 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 9 DP 15520)
  4. 5 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 8 DP: 15520)
  5. 6 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 7 DP 17153)
  6. 7 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 6A DP 17153)
  7. 8 Glencoe Road, Woollahra (Lot 4 DP 17153)
  8. 50 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot B DP 330100)
  9. 56 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 3 DP 17153)
  10. 58 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 5 DP 15520)
  11. 60 Wallaroy Road, Woollahra (Lot 6 DP 17153)
  1. That Council request the Minister for Planning and Public Spaces (or delegate) to authorise Council as the local plan-making authority in relation to the planning proposal, to make the local environmental plan under section 3.36 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979.

The Amendment was put and Lost.


For the AmendmentAgainst the Amendment

Councillor Dixson, Councillor Robertson, Councillor Witt, Councillor Regan
Councillor Carmichael, Councillor Mitchell, Councillor Torsten, Councillor Parmegiani

4/4


Note:

Note: 
The Committee amended Parts A and B, and added new Parts C, D and E to the Recommendation.

(Councillor Robertson/Councillor Torsten)

702/2025 Recommendation:

THAT Council:
 
  1. Notes the updated Street Tree Master Plan.

  2. Resolves to form a sub-committee to review the updated Street Tree Master Plan consisting of at least five councillors representing each municipal Ward, responsible for:

  1. Reviewing the updated Street Tree Masterplan as a whole including its aims and strategies.
  2. Reviewing the updated Plan’s Species Lists for their respective Ward including Proposed Species and Critical Comments.
  3. Engaging with local residents and resident groups in relation to the updated Street Tree Masterplan.
  4. Providing feedback and suggested changes arising from their review to Council officers by 2 February 2026.

  1. Notes that the sub-committee in suggesting any changes to the Street Tree Master Plan will not:

  1. Include new species that are not listed as part of the new tree palette.
  2. Include the use of species that are being retired from the Street Tree Master Plan palette.

  1. Requests Council officers to update and table changes to the Street Tree Master Plan at the March/April meeting of the Environmental Planning Committee with a view to its endorsement for public exhibition.

  2. Resolves to appoint the following Councillors to the sub-committee, representing their respective wards.

  1. Bellevue Hill Ward, Councillor Woodgate
  2. Cooper Ward, Councillor Mitchell and Councillor Torsten
  3. Double Bay Ward, Councillor Zeltzer
  4. Paddington Ward, Councillor Robertson
  5. Vaucluse Ward, Councillor Jarvis

The Motion was put and Carried.

Note:
In accordance with Council's Code of Meeting Practice a Division of votes is recorded on this matter.

For the MotionAgainst the Motion
